item.title: Solid-Earth geophysics and geodesy in Antarctica: achievements, current capabilities, and future directions
item.dc:creator: Mirko Scheinert, Weisen Shen, R. C. Aster, Lambert Caron, Michael D. Hartinger, Matt A. King, … (+22)
item.description:
Solid Earth — matched: ice sheet, cryosphere, Antarctic, Antarctica, mass loss, last glacial maximum, Holocene, sea level, sea-level rise, solid earth
The Antarctic Ice Sheet (AIS) plays a major role in the global climate, providing a natural laboratory to study the processes that interlink the cryosphere, solid Earth, atmosphere, and hydrosphere. Through its ongoing mass loss, the AIS currently contributes to global-mean sea-level rise at a rate of 0.4 mm a −1 . However, its impact on and feedback with climate and sea-level changes are still poorly understood. To generate reliable sea-level projections for the future, there is an urgent need to substantially improve our knowledge of the solid-Earth properties and subsequent response to ice-mass variations in space and time. This issue has been identified as a key question by the international community, strongly supported by the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research (SCAR). We review how state-of-the-art Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) and seismic networks in Antarctica, in combination with further ground-based, airborne and satellite-based geophysical measurements, have been used to significantly advance our understanding of solid-Earth processes and their impact on the cryosphere. Future research activities should be coordinated to answer the most urgent science questions. For example, how can we consistently test and model, respectively, a realistic mantle rheology that includes lateral inhomogeneity and transient relaxation, together with AIS mass changes on all time scales since the Last Glacial Maximum, including Holocene retreat and readvance? What processes and boundary conditions should coupled ice-sheet/gravity-rotation-deformation models include in order to realistically reflect the complex interaction between the solid Earth, ice sheet and ocean? Based on the recent achievements and the most urgent science questions, a vision is articulated for science-driven, multidisciplinary geophysical observations and corresponding technological developments. Long-term observations and improved modelling must be combined to develop precise and reliable projections for Antarctica's future mass change and associated contribution to sea-level change at both regional and global scales.

item.title: Research progress on the geomorphic evolution of the Taihu Lake Basin since the LGM and its implications for the human living environment
item.dc:creator: Yuhai Wang, 朱浦毅, 唐伟, Jun Kuang, Baoqiang He, Wei Zhang, … (+2)
item.description:
Frontiers in Earth Science — matched: last glacial maximum, LGM, Holocene, sea level, sea-level rise
The coupling between Neolithic cultural vicissitudes and paleogeomorphic evolution is a core issue in environmental archaeological research in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River. Based on a synthesis and analysis of advances in environmental archaeology over the past few decades, the study systematically reviews and evaluates key scientific issues such as sea-level changes in eastern China since the Last Glacial Maximum, the geomorphic evolution processes in the Taihu Lake Basin, and their impacts on the distribution of Neolithic sites, with a focus on discussing controversial issues such as the existence of the Holocene high sea-level stand, the genesis of the “present-day Taihu Lake”, and the causes of the collapse of the Liangzhu culture. In addition, by synthesizing the prehistoric subsistence strategies, the study offers new insights into the prospection of Neolithic sites predating 7 ka BP. The results demonstrate that the sea-level in East China commenced a period of rapid rise following the end of the LGM. The rate of rise then decreased at ∼7 ka BP, shifting to a slower rise phase with subsequent fluctuating upward trends. A mid-Holocene high sea-level stand occurred during ∼7–4 ka BP, with sea-level ∼2 m higher than present-day level. Furthermore, the geomorphic evolution of the Taihu Lake Basin stems from the long-term superimposition and coupling of multiple driving factors. It underwent successive stages of “paleosurface formation”, “hummocky terrace formation”, “chenier ridge formation”, and “dish-shaped depression formation”. During ∼7–3 ka BP, the area experienced a geomorphic reversal stage, evolving from a hummocky terrace toward a lake-plain landscape centered on dish-shaped depressions. The spatial distribution of Neolithic sites in this region closely responds to geomorphic and environmental changes, revealing a distinct human migration pattern: settlements shifted from uplands to plains and subsequently to high coastal areas. The collapse of the Liangzhu culture was primarily triggered by frequent flooding events, which were jointly induced by ENSO-enhanced precipitation variability and sea-level rise under cold and dry climatic conditions. Neolithic sites predating 7 ka BP may be preserved on elevated terraces and paleochannel terraces formed during the terminal LGM.

item.title: Oxygen isotopes reveal a significant Middle Pleistocene transition from temperate rainforest to arid desert-like conditions in eastern Australia
item.dc:creator: Christopher Laurikainen Gaete, Scott A. Hocknull, Andrew M. Lorrey, Katarina Maryann Mikac, Rochelle A. Lawrence, Anthony Dosseto
item.description:
Quaternary Science Reviews — matched: Quaternary, proxy, oxygen isotope, climate change
Reconstructing terrestrial palaeoenvironmental change during the Middle Pleistocene is essential for understanding ecosystem stability and resilience under long-term climatic forcing. However, well-dated, quantitative records from Australia remain limited. Fossil deposits at Mount Etna Caves, central eastern Queensland, preserve two taxonomically distinct faunal assemblages that have been interpreted as a substantial ecological transition from a diverse rainforest system to an arid-adapted faunal community. Previous interpretations of this transition have relied primarily on faunal evidence, with limited site-specific geochemical validation. Here, we integrate oxygen isotope (δ 18 O) analyses of fossil macropodid enamel with refined in-situ U-Th geochronology to reconstruct changes in hydroclimatic conditions across this transition. New U-Th ages better constrain deposition of the arid-adapted assemblage to a narrow interval between 199 ± 5 and 205 ± 4 ka. Fossils from older deposits (pre-280 ka) exhibit consistently low δ 18 O values (−2.59 ± 0.54 ‰), suggesting relatively humid conditions, whereas the younger deposit is markedly enriched (4.59 ± 1.92 ‰). Random Forest classification models trained on modern macropodine δ 18 O data suggest that pre-280 ka assemblages show strongest similarity with humid temperate forest environments analogous to modern temperate oceanic (Cfb-like) systems of southeastern Australia and highland New Guinea. In contrast, the post-205 ka assemblages show the strongest affinity with arid, hot desert (BWh-like) conditions characteristic of central Australia. This transition coincides with broader Middle Pleistocene climatic reorganisation centred on ∼270 ka, which may have contributed to sustained regional drying. These findings suggest that long-term climatic forcing may push ecosystems beyond hydroclimatic thresholds, resulting in major ecological reorganisation, altered species distributions, and reduced biogeographic connectivity. By providing a directly dated, multi-proxy terrestrial record, this study highlights how substantial environmental change during the Quaternary offers an important analogue for understanding ecosystem vulnerability under ongoing and future climate change.

item.title: Short-Campaign GNSS Observations of Horizontal Velocity and Vertical Tidal Response Across the Drygalski Ice Tongue, East Antarctica
item.dc:creator: Shahriar Mokhtari, Matteo Cappuccio, Antonio Zanutta, Luca Vittuari
item.description:
Remote Sensing — matched: glacier, Antarctica, polar
The Drygalski Ice Tongue is a tide-influenced floating extension of the David Glacier in East Antarctica, where field observations are constrained by polar logistics. We investigated how horizontal ice motion and vertical tidal response vary along and across the tongue. To extend earlier observations, we analysed a 2025–2026 Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) campaign comprising 12 stations and 248 station-days. Kinematic GNSS coordinate series were produced with Bernese 5.4 and subsequently analysed under four stochastic covariance descriptions for horizontal and apparent vertical-rate estimation. Comparisons with a regional Mario Zucchelli Station (MZS)/Terra Nova Bay tide reference characterized station-level up-component response to tidal forcing, and two tide-removal paths were evaluated for apparent vertical-rate analysis. Floating-tongue speeds increased downstream, spanning 663.9–749.4 m/yr, with a clockwise turn toward the southeast and north-to-south differences in fitted campaign rates. The main horizontal patterns persisted across all four tested covariance descriptions. Vertical tidal response was weak in the near-grounding group, spatially heterogeneous in the transition sector, and near-unity downstream. Across the four covariance descriptions, neither tide-removal approach yielded a model-robust apparent vertical-rate field. The campaign resolved spatial patterns of horizontal motion and vertical tidal response, while covariance testing identified the limits of apparent vertical-rate inference from short GNSS records.

item.title: Ground-Penetrating Radar Ice-Thickness Survey and 3D Bed-Topography Modelling of the Weigele Glacier Constrained by Borehole-Calibrated Radar Velocity
item.dc:creator: Jian Li, Yong Zhao, Yaxing Li, Yongming Jin, Sailajia Wei, Binjun Yao, … (+1)
item.description:
Applied Sciences — matched: subglacial, glacier
Glacier thickness and subglacial bed topography are fundamental parameters for ice-volume estimation of mountain glaciers; in regions where direct field observations are sparse, these parameters remain weakly constrained in space. This study deployed a closed-loop ground-penetrating radar (GPR) survey network on Weigele Glacier in the Animaqing Mountains and calibrated the radar wave velocity using a GPR profile that crossed an in situ borehole. The borehole-calibrated effective radar wave velocity is 0.17018 m·ns−1, which is 1.30% higher than the commonly used default value of 0.168 m·ns−1. Based on 1477 GPR ice-thickness measurements and zero-thickness boundary points at the upper glacier margin, Gaussian process regression was used to interpolate ice thickness on a 5 m horizontal grid. Leave-one-profile-out cross-validation showed that adding the ice-surface slope covariate changed the model error only slightly (RMSE of 85.48 m) relative to the coordinate-only baseline model (RMSE of 85.44 m); the final reconstruction therefore adopted horizontal coordinates as predictors. Within the 0.481 km2 GPR modelling domain, the maximum measured ice thickness is 258.328 m, the mean interpolated ice thickness is 130.10 m, and the ice volume is 0.06260 km3. The reconstructed bed exhibits a pronounced longitudinal trough, and the low-lying bed corresponds spatially to the main thick-ice zone. Boundary-condition sensitivity tests yield an ice-volume range of 0.04767–0.07531 km3. These volume estimates correspond to the modelling domain covered by the GPR network.

item.title: Historical Multidecadal Variability of Intraseasonal Features of Sahel Rainfall in CMIP6 Models and Observations
item.dc:creator: Pablo Fernández, Juliette Mignot, Alessandra Giannini, Elsa Mohíno, Guillaume Gastineau, F. Hourdin
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: CMIP, ensemble
Abstract We compare observations with seven large ensembles of CMIP6 historical simulations to understand the role that external forcings and internal variability may have played in modulating the frequency and intensity of daily rainfall, and the duration of the rainy season in the Sahel. We compare three periods: [1950–1970], [1970–1990] and [1994–2014]. The results show that the anomalously wet [1950–1970] and [1994–2014] periods are characterized by more extreme rainfall days and longer monsoon seasons than the drier [1970–1990] period. In exploring the contributions of anthropogenic aerosols (AAs) and greenhouse gases (GHGs) in both transitions, we find results to be consistent with partial cancellation of the effects of AA and GHG in the [1950–1970] to [1970–1990] transition to drought, which allows internal variability to contribute significantly, and with the emergence of the external forcing effect in the [1970–1990] to [1994–2014] recovery. In particular, the shift of AA emissions from North America and Europe to Asia between [1970–1990] and [1994–2014] increases the number of extreme rainy days and lengthens the wet season. The increase in GHG concentrations between these two periods also acts to increase the number of extreme rainy days. However, this effect is not statistically significant in all models. Finally, in all the models analyzed, we cannot discard the fact that the individual effects of AAs and GHGs add up linearly in setting the total precipitation change.

item.title: Discrepancies and Consistencies in Multi-Source Estimates of Eurasian Spring Snowmelt During 1982–2014
item.dc:creator: Yutong Zhang, Juan Zhou, Xing Li, Lixia Meng, Yangruixue Chen, Xiao Li, … (+1)
item.description:
Remote Sensing — matched: albedo, uncertainty quantification
Snow alters land–atmosphere energy and moisture exchanges via albedo and hydrological effects, markedly impacting subseasonal-to-seasonal climate variability. While Earth observations and model-based products form the foundation for investigating snow–climate interactions, comprehensive assessments of snowmelt, which directly reflects snow-induced hydrological and thermal anomalies, remain scarce compared to those of conventional snow mass variables. Benchmarked against the satellite–in situ blended GlobSnow data, this study comprehensively evaluates the discrepancies and consistencies of Eurasian spring snowmelt (spring snow water equivalent difference, SSD) across six multi-source datasets (SnowCCI, JRA-3Q, ERA5-Land, MERRA-2, GLDAS-NOAH, and FLDAS) during 1982–2014. The results reveal that satellite-based SnowCCI and JRA-3Q exhibit the highest consistency with GlobSnow in reproducing the spatial distribution, temporal variability, and dominant east–west dipole mode of Eurasian SSD. Specifically, they accurately capture its clear latitudinal zonation and a distinct dipole-like trend, characterized by decreasing SSD over western Eurasia and increasing SSD over eastern Eurasia. Conversely, ERA5-Land and MERRA-2 reasonably capture the temporal evolution of SSD but tend to overestimate variability amplitudes. GLDAS-NOAH exhibits relatively weak regional heterogeneity and underestimates SSD variability, whereas FLDAS tends to overestimate variability amplitudes and shows pronounced regional dependence. Further analysis suggests that uncertainties in snowfall simulations may be a major source of discrepancies in SSD estimation, although their relative contribution remains uncertain. These findings provide crucial insights for selecting appropriate datasets in snow–climate research and underscore the importance of dataset uncertainty quantification in subseasonal-to-seasonal climate prediction.
